Russian Hackers Exploit Microsoft OWA Flaw to Keep Mailbox Access After Credential Rotation
thehackernews.com · 30 Jul 2026 07:40 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.5
TAGScl-sta-1114cross-site-scriptingdns-tunnelingeuropehalf-click-exploitlaundry-bearmicrosoftoauth-token-theftowareaperrussiata488united-statesvoid-blizzardzimbrazimreaper
96
In plain words

Russian hackers known as Laundry Bear are using a flaw in Microsoft Outlook Web Access to break into email accounts when a person simply opens a specially crafted message. The campaign has targeted U.S. and European government groups, as well as telecommunications, financial, hospitality, and aerospace organizations. It matters because the malicious code can keep access to a victim’s mailbox even after passwords are changed or the person’s device is rebuilt, giving the attackers a lasting way to read sensitive email.

Summary
Russian-linked Laundry Bear/TA488 is exploiting a Microsoft Outlook Web Access XSS flaw to deploy OWAReaper, a browser-based implant that can persist even after password resets or device reimaging. The campaign targets government and major industries in the U.S. and Europe using emails that trigger compromise simply when viewed in vulnerable OWA.

Russian threat actors linked to prior Zimbra exploitation have been observed exploiting CVE-2026-42897, a now-patched cross-site scripting flaw in Microsoft Outlook Web Access. Proofpoint attributed the activity to Laundry Bear, also known as TA488, CL-STA-1114, UNK_PitStop, and Void Blizzard. The campaign began on July 22, 2026, and targeted U.S. and European government entities as well as the telecommunications, financial, hospitality, and aerospace sectors.

The attacks use compromised accounts to send vague informational emails that do not require the recipient to click a link or open an attachment. If the message is viewed in a vulnerable version of OWA, JavaScript embedded in the email can trigger the exploit and assemble the next-stage payload. Proofpoint described this as part of TA488’s continued use of “half-click” exploits, where opening the email is enough to cause compromise.

The campaign deploys OWAReaper, a previously unknown JavaScript browser-based implant built for persistent access inside Microsoft’s webmail client. OWAReaper can store itself in browser localStorage, abuse OWA’s offline IndexedDB message cache, and use mailbox permissions to maintain access even after credential rotation or full device re-imaging. It can receive commands through GitHub commit messages or attacker-sent emails and exfiltrate data over HTTPS or, if that fails, through DNS label tunneling.

  • Credential rotation and even full device re-imaging are insufficient remediation for OWAReaper because the article says its server-side mailbox permissions require deliberate removal from the Exchange server.
  • The phishing messages are intentionally generic and lack links or attachments, making ordinary user caution less effective because simply opening and reading the message in vulnerable OWA can trigger compromise.
  • OWAReaper removes the exploit content from the email on the Exchange server after execution, which can make later investigation harder by altering the original malicious message.
  • The campaign’s early infrastructure was created in March 2026, two months before Microsoft disclosed CVE-2026-42897, which Proofpoint said raises the possibility that the flaw may have been exploited as a zero-day.
  • OWAReaper’s use of both GitHub commit messages and attacker-sent emails for commands gives the operators backup communication paths if one method is disrupted.
Key Points
  • 01Proofpoint observed Russian threat actor Laundry Bear, also known as TA488, exploiting CVE-2026-42897, a cross-site scripting vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook Web Access, to target U.S. and European government entities and organizations in the telecommunications, financial, hospitality, and aerospace sectors.
  • 02The campaign began on July 22, 2026, and used compromised accounts to send generic emails that required no clicks or attachments because viewing the message in a vulnerable OWA client could trigger the exploit.
  • 03The attacks deploy OWAReaper, a previously unknown JavaScript browser-based implant that runs inside the OWA reading pane and is described as an evolution of ZimReaper.
  • 04OWAReaper can persist through browser reboots, credential rotation, and full device re-imaging by storing itself in browser localStorage, abusing OWA offline cache behavior, and granting server-side mailbox permissions when conditions allow.
  • 05OWAReaper supports command-and-control through GitHub commit messages or attacker-sent emails, and exfiltrates data over HTTPS with AES-CTR encrypted URI paths or, if that fails, through DNS label tunneling.

This is a must-read because it reports active exploitation in the wild of a Microsoft Outlook Web Access vulnerability by a named Russian threat actor targeting government and major industry sectors. The described OWAReaper implant is high-impact because it can maintain mailbox access after credential rotation and device re-imaging, making remediation more difficult.

VMware fixes three critical flaws allowing auth bypass, VM escapes
bleepingcomputer.com · 30 Jul 2026 18:00 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.5
TAGSauthentication-bypassbrickstormbroadcomchinacisacve-2026-47876cve-2026-59309cve-2026-59310directory-traversalvirtualghostvm-escapevmwarevmware-esxivmware-vcentervmxnet3
95
In plain words

Broadcom released urgent fixes for serious security problems in VMware software used to run and manage many virtual servers, including vCenter, ESX, Workstation, and Fusion. Organizations using affected versions are told to update right away because the flaws could let attackers get into management systems without signing in, run their own code, or break out from a virtual machine to the main server. This matters because VMware systems often control large parts of an organization’s servers and data, and criminals have commonly targeted them in past attacks.

Summary
Broadcom released emergency VMware updates fixing three critical flaws in vCenter and ESXi, including authentication bypass, remote code execution, and a VM escape via VMXNET3. Admins should patch immediately because there are no workarounds, though Broadcom says it has not seen active exploitation yet.

Broadcom released security updates for five vulnerabilities in VMware vCenter, ESX, Workstation, and Fusion, including three critical flaws. The affected products also include VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation, VMware Telco Cloud Platform, and VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure because they contain vCenter or ESX. Broadcom says organizations running versions released before the fixed versions in its advisory should assume they are vulnerable and take immediate action.

The critical flaws include CVE-2026-59309, an authentication bypass in VMware Directory Service, CVE-2026-59310, a directory traversal issue in the vCenter Syslog server that can allow arbitrary code execution, and CVE-2026-47876, an out-of-bounds write in the VMXNET3 virtual network adapter that can allow a virtual machine escape. Broadcom says there are no workarounds and is treating the fixes as emergency changes, though it has no indication the vulnerabilities are being exploited in the wild. Patching vCenter can temporarily interrupt access to management interfaces, while ESX updates require a server restart and may require moving or powering down virtual machines.

  • Broadcom explicitly advises against switching virtual machines away from VMXNET3 as a mitigation because other virtual network adapters have also had security flaws and may reduce performance.
  • Patching vCenter will temporarily interrupt access to the vSphere Client and other management interfaces, but running virtual machines and containers will continue operating during the update.
  • ESX updates require a host restart, so Broadcom recommends using vMotion and rolling reboots where possible, while virtual machines that cannot be migrated must be powered down.
  • The new vSphere 8.0 and 9.0 patches can block planned upgrades to VMware Cloud Foundation 9.x with a “back in time” error until later releases restore upgrade compatibility.
  • Supported environments can use ESX Live Patch to reduce disruption for ESX updates, but the vCenter updates are not eligible for Quick Patch.
Key Points
  • 01Broadcom released security updates for five vulnerabilities in VMware vCenter, ESX, Workstation, and Fusion, including three critical flaws that allow authentication bypass, arbitrary code execution, or virtual machine escape.
  • 02The affected products also include VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation, VMware Telco Cloud Platform, and VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure because they contain vCenter or ESX.
  • 03The three critical vulnerabilities are CVE-2026-59309 and CVE-2026-59310 in vCenter, both rated CVSS 9.8, and CVE-2026-47876 in the VMXNET3 virtual network adapter, rated CVSS 9.3.
  • 04Broadcom says there are no workarounds for the vulnerabilities and is treating the fixes as emergency changes that administrators should install as soon as possible.
  • 05Broadcom says it has no indication that the vulnerabilities are being exploited in the wild, but VMware servers are commonly targeted because compromising vCenter or ESXi can provide access to large portions of an organization’s servers and data.

    Hackers Exploit AnySign4PC via Hacked Korean Sites to Install Backdoors Without Prompts
    thehackernews.com · 30 Jul 2026 10:33 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.5

    In plain words

    South Korean authorities and security companies say a state-sponsored group broke into trusted Korean websites and used them to infect visitors who had vulnerable AnySign4PC financial-security software installed, without asking the visitor to download or approve anything. The affected people and organizations include those in South Korea that visited these compromised sites while running AnySign4PC versions 1.1.4.4 through 1.1.4.6, with evidence of related attacks at 72 organizations in 2026. This matters because ordinary visits to familiar websites could let attackers secretly take control of computers, steal files, explore internal networks, and install more harmful tools, including links to attacks that ended in Gunra ransomware.

    Summary
    South Korean authorities say state-sponsored hackers compromised trusted local websites to silently exploit vulnerable AnySign4PC financial-security software and install SIGNBT or COPPERHEDGE backdoors on visitors’ systems. Users should remove or update AnySign4PC versions 1.1.4.4 through 1.1.4.6 to version 1.1.5.0 and hunt for signs of in-memory backdoors, DLL side-loading, and suspicious SSH tunneling.

    South Korean authorities and four security firms disclosed a state-sponsored campaign that compromised trusted domestic websites. The attackers used those sites to exploit locally installed financial-security software and infect targeted visitors with SIGNBT or COPPERHEDGE backdoors. KISA said AnySign4PC versions 1.1.4.4 through 1.1.4.6 are affected and lists version 1.1.5.0 as the fixed release.

    A compromised page could infect a system running a vulnerable AnySign4PC version without a prompt or user-initiated download. AhnLab said it identified evidence of related attacks at 72 organizations in 2026 and found 15 legitimate websites used as watering holes. The company also found overlap with attacks that ended with Gunra ransomware, but said the evidence does not establish that one actor conducted both operations.

    AhnLab described an exploit chain that used four PNG images to exchange keys, check the installed software version, deliver version-specific exploit code, and report whether execution succeeded. The malicious page communicated with the local security program over WebSocket and triggered a buffer overflow to execute shellcode, after which payloads were injected into legitimate Microsoft processes. The reports recommend hunting for suspicious DLL loading, encrypted service-registry data, in-memory Portable Executable execution, unusual service creation, injection into SyncHost.exe or svchost.exe, and unexpected outbound SSH tunnels.

    • A single page visit could be enough for compromise because the malicious page communicated with the local AnySign4PC component over WebSocket and triggered code execution without a user download or prompt.
    • The article cautions that AhnLab’s figure of 72 affected organizations is not a count of equally confirmed full compromises, because the report does not state what evidence qualified an organization for inclusion.
    • Attribution is deliberately limited: the advisory and Operation Double Barrel report describe a state-sponsored group but do not formally attribute the overall 2025–2026 campaign or the Gunra-linked intrusions to Lazarus.
    • The malware’s behavior makes stable file indicators less reliable, because ENKI found one backdoor mode could delete its registry configuration, loader, and backdoor files after copying them into memory and later restore a loader with a different hash.
    • The Gunra overlap is technically significant but inconclusive, with AhnLab listing possibilities such as shared tools, shared infrastructure, a common access broker, or access to the same operational resources rather than asserting a single operator.
    Key Points
    • 01South Korean authorities and four security firms disclosed a state-sponsored campaign that compromised trusted domestic websites to exploit locally installed financial-security software and install SIGNBT or COPPERHEDGE backdoors.
    • 02KISA said AnySign4PC versions 1.1.4.4 through 1.1.4.6 are affected by a buffer overflow that permits remote code execution, and it lists version 1.1.5.0 as the fixed release.
    • 03AhnLab said it found evidence of related attacks at 72 organizations in 2026 and identified 15 legitimate websites used as watering holes.
    • 04AhnLab reported overlap between the state-sponsored activity and attacks that ended with Gunra ransomware, including shared vulnerabilities, filenames, an SSH key fingerprint, and network infrastructure, but said the evidence does not prove one actor conducted both operations.
    • 05The reports recommend hunting for behavior such as suspicious DLL loading by legitimate executables, encrypted data in service-registry entries, in-memory Portable Executable execution, injection into SyncHost.exe or svchost.exe, and unexpected outbound SSH tunnels.

In plain words

South Korean security agencies and AhnLab say North Korea’s Lazarus Group appears to be using the same tools and computer servers as the Gunra extortion group, which locks victims’ files and demands money. They targeted South Korean organizations, including government agencies, cryptocurrency exchanges, IT service providers, and other companies, by abusing widely used Korean financial security software. This matters because people may be infected just by visiting a legitimate website that attackers have secretly tampered with, especially if they have outdated software on their computers. The findings also suggest North Korean government hackers may be helping criminal extortion groups, widening the risk beyond the original targets.

Summary
South Korean agencies and AhnLab warn that North Korea’s Lazarus Group appears to be sharing tools, infrastructure, and access with the Gunra ransomware operation, with both exploiting Korean financial security software to target South Korean organizations. The overlap suggests Pyongyang-backed hackers may be supplying ransomware criminals rather than merely acting as affiliates.

South Korean security and intelligence agencies warned that cyberattack tools and infrastructure used by North Korea’s Lazarus Group appear to have been shared with ransomware criminals targeting South Korean organizations. AhnLab’s technical report says Lazarus and the Gunra ransomware scheme ran parallel campaigns from 2025 through the first half of 2026, differing mainly in their final objective. Lazarus installed espionage backdoors in at least 72 organizations in 2026 alone, while Gunra used access to encrypt files, steal data, and demand extortion payments.

AhnLab found both groups exploited the same vulnerabilities in Korean financial security software products that are effectively mandatory for Korean banking or government services. The groups also used identical malware filenames and execution arguments, the same privilege escalation tools, the same command-and-control servers, the same SSH key fingerprint, and the same method for deleting malware. AhnLab named the campaign “Operation Double Barrel” and assessed a high likelihood of technical linkage, while saying the overlaps could indicate collaboration, shared infrastructure, or access brokering.

The attackers compromised 15 legitimate Korean websites and used them for watering-hole attacks that could infect visitors with outdated security software. They also conducted spearphishing, including emails to a Korean defense company disguised as a survey about GaN semiconductors, and AhnLab said some lure pages appeared to be AI-generated. The findings add to evidence that North Korean state-sponsored actors are becoming more entangled with ransomware operations, with the Gunra connection potentially suggesting state hackers supplied tools, exploits, and access to a newer group.

  • The overlap between Lazarus and Gunra may represent a reversal of earlier North Korean ransomware activity, with state hackers potentially supplying tools, exploits, and access to a newer criminal group rather than joining an established ransomware franchise as affiliates.
  • The abused Korean financial security software creates risk beyond high-value organizations because it is also installed on many personal PCs and can be triggered when a user visits a specific compromised page.
  • AhnLab assessed that several watering-hole sites may have been compromised through a shared Korean website development company’s management system, showing how one provider compromise could expose multiple client websites.
  • The use of identical SSH key fingerprints, command-and-control servers, privilege escalation tools, and cleanup methods gave AhnLab enough evidence to classify the campaigns as having a high likelihood of technical linkage, even though it did not definitively attribute both campaigns to one actor.
  • The attackers’ lure activity included emails disguised as a GaN semiconductor survey sent to a Korean defense company, and AhnLab noted that some lure pages appeared to have been generated with AI.
Key Points
  • 01AhnLab reported that North Korea’s Lazarus Group and the Gunra ransomware scheme ran parallel campaigns against South Korean targets from 2025 through the first half of 2026, differing mainly in their final objective.
  • 02Both groups exploited the same vulnerabilities in Korean financial security software products that are widely required for Korean banking or government services.
  • 03AhnLab found overlaps including identical malware filenames and execution arguments, the same privilege escalation tools, the same command-and-control servers, and the same SSH key fingerprint.
  • 04The attackers compromised 15 legitimate Korean websites across multiple industries and used them for watering-hole attacks that redirected selected visitors to infrastructure that triggered the software flaws.
  • 05South Korean security and intelligence agencies warned that individuals and organizations may be infected simply by visiting a compromised legitimate website, especially if outdated security software is installed.

The impact spans government agencies, cryptocurrency exchanges, IT service providers, enterprises, and personal PCs, with infection possible through compromised legitimate websites.

JetBrains warns of critical TeamCity remote code execution flaw

In plain words

JetBrains warned that all self-hosted TeamCity servers have a serious flaw that could let someone get in without a password and run commands on the server. TeamCity Cloud customers do not need to do anything because JetBrains has already applied protections for them. This matters because TeamCity is used to build, test, and deploy software, and a successful break-in could expose data, settings, stored passwords, or tamper with software build and delivery systems.

Summary
JetBrains warned that all TeamCity On-Premises versions are affected by a critical authentication bypass flaw, CVE-2026-63077, that can enable remote code execution. Admins should urgently upgrade to fixed versions 2025.11.7 or 2026.1.3, or install the security patch plugin if they cannot upgrade.

JetBrains warned of a critical authentication bypass vulnerability affecting TeamCity On-Premises. The issue is tracked as CVE-2026-63077 and can be exploited by an attacker with HTTPS access to a TeamCity server. JetBrains said all versions of TeamCity On-Premises are affected, while TeamCity Cloud customers do not need to take action because the necessary measures have already been applied.

The flaw can be used through the agent polling protocol to bypass authentication and execute arbitrary operating system commands with the privileges of the server process. JetBrains said successful exploitation could expose TeamCity data, configurations, stored credentials, or compromise build artifacts and CI/CD pipelines, depending on privileges. At the time the advisory was published on July 27, JetBrains said there was no evidence of active exploitation.

JetBrains said the issue was privately reported on July 10 and was addressed in TeamCity versions 2025.11.7 and 2026.1.3. The vendor recommends upgrading to those versions, and it also provides a security patch plugin for TeamCity 2017.1 and later for customers unable to upgrade. JetBrains also recommended protective layers for internet-facing TeamCity servers and noted that even exposing the login page or REST API can give attackers an entry point to exploit newly disclosed vulnerabilities.

  • JetBrains recommends placing internet-facing TeamCity servers behind protective layers such as VPN access because even exposing only the login page or REST API can create an entry point for newly disclosed vulnerabilities.
  • Customers who cannot upgrade still have a mitigation path because JetBrains provides the security patch as a plugin for TeamCity 2017.1 and later.
  • TeamCity 2024.03 and newer can automatically download available security patch plugins and notify administrators, but administrators still need to install them.
  • Older TeamCity versions from 2017.1 through 2018.1 require a server restart after installing the patch plugin before the security update takes effect.
  • Administrators are urged to act quickly even though there was no active exploitation at publication time because past TeamCity flaws have been widely used by ransomware gangs and state-backed actors.
Key Points
  • 01JetBrains warned of a critical authentication bypass vulnerability in TeamCity On-Premises, tracked as CVE-2026-63077, that could allow remote code execution.
  • 02All versions of TeamCity On-Premises are affected, while TeamCity Cloud customers do not need to take action because JetBrains has already applied the necessary measures.
  • 03An attacker with HTTPS access to a TeamCity server could exploit the flaw through the agent polling protocol to run operating system commands with the privileges of the server process.
  • 04JetBrains said successful exploitation could expose TeamCity data, configurations, stored credentials, or compromise build artifacts and CI/CD pipelines, depending on privileges.
  • 05JetBrains addressed the issue in TeamCity versions 2025.11.7 and 2026.1.3 and also provides a security patch plugin for TeamCity 2017.1 and later for customers unable to upgrade.

In plain words

A criminal extortion group called Cl0p appears to have stolen confidential information from organizations using PTC’s Windchill and FlexPLM software, which companies use to manage product design and manufacturing work. The software is used by organizations in areas such as aerospace and defense, energy, electronics, medical technology, apparel, retail, and industrial systems. This matters because the stolen data may include product designs, specifications, supplier details, and other valuable company know-how, not just employee or customer records.

Summary
Cl0p is exploiting a critical PTC Windchill and FlexPLM remote code execution flaw, likely as a zero-day, to steal sensitive engineering and manufacturing data from exposed enterprise systems. Organizations using these products should patch immediately and remove public Internet exposure where possible.

PTC disclosed a critical remote code execution vulnerability, CVE-2026-12569, affecting Windchill and the FlexPLM add-on on June 17, 2026. Ransom-ISAC later reported that multiple organizations began receiving emails confirmed to be from the Cl0p ransom and extortion group, warning that confidential information had been stolen. The article says this vulnerability was likely exploited in early June 2026 as a zero-day, and CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on June 25, 2026.

The campaign is significant because Windchill and FlexPLM are used for product lifecycle and manufacturing processes, and PTC’s customer base includes organizations in aerospace and defense, electronics, energy, industrial systems, and medical technology. The article notes that data in these systems may include product designs, specifications, bills of materials, supplier and vendor data, and other intellectual property. Censys observed fewer than 100 Internet-exposed Windchill instances, showing that even a relatively small exposure footprint can still be valuable to attackers.

Censys analyzed exposed Windchill infrastructure, PTC-published indicators of compromise, and Cl0p’s updated contact infrastructure. About 80% of observed Windchill instances were in the United States, and nearly a quarter of underlying hosts were on Akamai infrastructure. PTC published 12 IP addresses and one CIDR range associated with the campaign, and Censys observed rapid service churn across some of those IPs during the suspected early-to-mid-June attack timeframe. Cl0p also announced new contact domains, cryptohox.com and cypherhex.com, which were registered on July 17, 2026 and hosted mail infrastructure including Roundcube Webmail.

  • This campaign shows that a small Internet-exposed footprint can still be highly attractive to extortion actors when the exposed systems hold high-value engineering, manufacturing, and intellectual property data.
  • The decline in exposed Windchill instances shortly after PTC’s advisory suggests that some operators responded by taking systems offline, reinforcing that removing public exposure is a practical mitigation beyond patching.
  • Censys observed some campaign-associated services appearing and disappearing in less than 24 hours, making timely detection and historical visibility important for investigating this activity.
  • One listed IOC, 78.128.113.10, showed Platypus C2 tooling that the article says is not a known Cl0p technique and may be unrelated, so defenders should validate indicators rather than treating every listed host as equally attributable.
  • Cl0p’s new contact domains look operationally ordinary without their known association to the group, because they use common mail services and current Roundcube Webmail versions, making reputation and context important for identifying them.
Key Points
  • 01PTC disclosed a critical remote code execution vulnerability, CVE-2026-12569, affecting Windchill and the FlexPLM add-on on June 17, 2026.
  • 02Ransom-ISAC reported that beginning July 20, 2026, multiple organizations received emails confirmed to be from the Cl0p extortion group claiming that confidential information had been stolen.
  • 03Censys observed fewer than 100 Internet-exposed PTC Windchill instances as far back as June 1, 2026, with a decline in exposed instances after PTC’s June 17 advisory.
  • 04PTC published 12 IP addresses associated with the campaign, and Censys observed rapid service churn across some of those IPs during the suspected early-to-mid-June attack timeframe.
  • 05Cl0p’s new contact domains, cryptohox.com and cypherhex.com, were registered on July 17, 2026, and hosted mail infrastructure with Roundcube Webmail.

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-60004) Gitea Remote Code Execution via diffpatch Git Hooks
cycognito.com · 30 Jul 2026 10:39 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.5
TAGScve-2026-60004cycognitodiffpatch-apigitgit-hooksgiteagitea-cloudnight-rang3rpost-index-change

In plain words

The article explains a critical flaw in Gitea, a self-hosted service used to store and manage software code, where a specially submitted change can make the server run commands chosen by an attacker. Self-managed Gitea versions from 1.17 up to 1.27.1 are affected, especially default setups that let anyone create an account and make a repository. This matters because these servers can hold source code, passwords, deployment keys, database access, and other sensitive company secrets. The fix is to upgrade to Gitea 1.27.1, while temporary steps include turning off public sign-ups and blocking the risky feature.

Summary
Gitea versions 1.17 through 1.27.0 are affected by a critical remote code execution flaw, CVE-2026-60004, that can let an attacker with repository write access execute commands via malicious diffpatch content installed as a Git hook. Self-managed instances should upgrade to Gitea 1.27.1 immediately and disable open registration or block the diffpatch route until patched.

CVE-2026-60004 is a critical code injection vulnerability in Gitea that allows attacker-controlled patch content to be installed and executed as a Git hook on the server. The flaw affects every Gitea release from 1.17 up to but not including 1.27.1, and Gitea Cloud instances were stated to be upgraded automatically. Exploitation requires repository write access, but Gitea’s default configuration leaves registration open and places no repository creation limit, which can let an anonymous visitor obtain the needed access on an unmodified installation.

The vulnerability is in the POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/diffpatch endpoint, where Gitea applies submitted patches inside a shared bare temporary clone. Submitting the same patch twice can trigger a Git three-way fallback that writes a file into the bare clone’s hooks directory, causing Git to execute it while writing the index. Successful exploitation runs commands as the Gitea operating system account and can expose application secrets, environment variables, repositories, database credentials and contents, OAuth and integration credentials, and other internal or reachable services.

Gitea 1.27.1, released on July 27, 2026, fixes the issue by changing the temporary clone from bare to non-bare, and the article states that upgrading to 1.27.1 is the only complete fix. The article also notes that the release notes listed the change under MISC rather than SECURITY, with the security advisory following a day later. Until upgrading is confirmed, recommended actions include inventorying Gitea instances, disabling open registration, blocking the diffpatch API route, using a noexec temporary directory where possible, auditing write grants, and monitoring for unexpected child processes of the Gitea service account.

  • The vulnerability is especially risky on default Gitea installations because open registration can turn a flaw that normally needs repository write access into one reachable by an anonymous visitor who creates an account and repository.
  • Teams that prioritize upgrades based on security-labeled release notes could miss the fix because Gitea 1.27.1 listed the relevant change under MISC and the security advisory was published a day later.
  • The article emphasizes that the most exposed Gitea servers may be hard to find internally because they are often developer-run, contractor-created, inherited through acquisitions, or otherwise outside formal inventories.
  • Disabling open registration is only a temporary risk reduction step because it does not protect against existing users who already have repository write access.
  • The proof of concept does not require an outbound callback because command output can be stored in Git objects and retrieved over authenticated smart HTTP.
Key Points
  • 01CVE-2026-60004 is a critical Gitea code injection vulnerability in the POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/diffpatch endpoint that can allow attacker-controlled patch content to be installed and executed as a Git hook on the server.
  • 02Exploitation requires repository write access, but Gitea’s default configuration allows open registration, no email confirmation or administrator approval, unrestricted new accounts, and no repository creation limit, allowing an anonymous visitor to obtain the needed access on an unmodified installation.
  • 03Every Gitea release from 1.17 up to but not including 1.27.1 is affected, while Gitea Cloud instances were stated to be automatically upgraded by the vendor.
  • 04Successful exploitation runs commands as the Gitea operating system account and can expose app.ini, application secrets, environment variables, mounted repositories, database credentials and contents, OAuth and integration credentials, and other services.
  • 05Gitea 1.27.1 fixes the vulnerability by changing the temporary clone from bare to non-bare, and the article says upgrading to 1.27.1 is the only complete fix.

The article also highlights that default open registration can make exploitation much easier on unmodified installations and provides concrete mitigations until upgrade.

    In plain words

    Amazon says a North Korea-linked hacker group tricked trusted software maintainers into letting them publish harmful updates to widely used JavaScript code packages, including axios, debug, chalk and typo-crypto. Developers and organizations that automatically installed the newest versions could have unknowingly downloaded malware into their web applications and business services. This matters because one poisoned open-source package can affect many companies at once, and the article says North Korea uses cyber theft, including cryptocurrency theft, to raise money despite international sanctions.

    Summary
    Amazon says North Korea-linked SapphireSleet was behind multiple NPM supply-chain compromises, including attacks on axios, chalk, debug and typo-crypto. The group used social engineering to take over trusted maintainers and push malicious updates that could reach thousands of downstream users.

    Amazon said the North Korea-linked hacker group SapphireSleet was responsible for several high-profile compromises of open-source JavaScript packages hosted on the NPM repository. The affected packages included typo-crypto in March 2025, debug and chalk in September 2025, and axios in March 2026. Axios is one of the world’s most widely used JavaScript libraries, downloaded more than 100 million times each week and embedded in many web applications and enterprise services.

    Amazon said the attackers gained access in each case by socially engineering a trusted maintainer before publishing a malicious update. Organizations that automatically installed the latest versions unknowingly downloaded malware. Amazon reported the malware used in the campaign to the Open Source Vulnerabilities database, where it is tracked as MAL-2026-3400.

    The axios compromise had previously been attributed to North Korean hackers by Google and linked by Microsoft to Sapphire Sleet, which overlaps with activity tracked by several other names. Amazon said the earlier package compromises had not previously been publicly linked to the same threat actor. The company said open-source repositories are attractive targets because compromising a few widely used packages can potentially affect thousands of downstream environments at once.

    • The campaign shows that automatically installing the newest open-source package versions can create exposure when a maintainer account is socially engineered.
    • Amazon emphasized that compromising a few widely used open-source packages can give attackers potential access to thousands of downstream environments instead of requiring separate intrusions into each organization.

    In plain words

    Amazon says North Korea was behind earlier tampering with popular npm software packages called debug and chalk, and links it to a later compromise of axios, but the article notes that Amazon has not fully shown which evidence connects the incidents. These packages are used by many software projects, so poisoned updates can quietly reach huge numbers of websites and apps, including code that tried to change cryptocurrency payment addresses before users approved transactions. The story matters because it shows how attackers can target trusted software maintainers and then spread harmful code through widely used building blocks, while new npm protections only reduce some of those paths and do not stop all of them.

    Summary
    Amazon attributed the 2025 npm hijacks of debug and chalk to North Korea’s Sapphire Sleet, linking them to the later axios compromise, but the article says the published evidence for that connection remains incomplete. The incidents highlight that npm supply-chain attacks still hinge on maintainer compromise even as newer npm protections reduce some install-script abuse.

    Amazon has attributed the September 2025 hijack of the npm packages debug and chalk to North Korea, assessing with medium confidence that the group behind the March 2026 axios compromise was also responsible. The original Aikido and Wiz reports on the debug and chalk incident did not attribute it to North Korea, and the article notes that Amazon’s evidence for linking the incidents is not fully detailed. The affected packages were part of a broader npm supply-chain compromise involving at least 18 packages with more than 2 billion weekly downloads combined.

    Amazon also linked the activity to typo-crypto, a small npm package published in March 2025 that contained a trojanized core.js file and is described by Amazon as a test run before attacks on more popular packages. The article says the package’s registry record does not fit Amazon’s characterization of a maintainer compromise followed by a malicious update, because it had only one version and appeared to impersonate crypto-js from its first publish. The malicious file used a trigger beginning 0098273, an XOR key of 01042025, and the network indicators npmjs[.]store and 216[.]74[.]123[.]126.

    The debug and chalk compromise used browser-side code that hooked fetch, XMLHttpRequest, and wallet APIs to rewrite cryptocurrency transaction addresses before users signed, and it left no persistence on the machine. Unlike the axios payload, that attack did not rely on an npm post-install hook, and Aikido confirmed the mechanism split between the incidents. The article notes that npm v12 now disables dependency lifecycle scripts by default and npm has begun scanning newly published packages for malware, but those measures do not close the maintainer-compromise path used in these incidents.

    • Amazon’s characterization of typo-crypto as part of a pattern of maintainer compromise conflicts with the registry record described in the article, which shows only one version published and no earlier benign release to update.
    • The debug and chalk payload did not use install or lifecycle scripts, so npm v12’s default blocking of dependency lifecycle scripts would not address that specific attack mechanism.
    • The malicious typo-crypto version was still published and installable when The Hacker News checked the registry on July 30, 2026, even though OSV had published MAL-2026-3400 nearly three months earlier.
    • Amazon’s published hash information for typo-crypto appears internally inconsistent according to the article, because one listed hash is actually for core.js and the stated core.js hash does not match any file in the tarball.
    • The article highlights a timing gap in attribution: axios was publicly attributed to North Korean activity within two days, while debug and chalk and typo-crypto were attributed ten and sixteen months later.
    Key Points
    • 01Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with medium confidence that the group behind the March 2026 axios compromise was also behind the September 2025 hijack of the npm packages debug and chalk.
    • 02The September 2025 debug and chalk compromise involved a maintainer phished through a lookalike npm domain and a wallet-draining script pushed into at least 18 packages with more than 2 billion weekly downloads combined.

In plain words

Amazon says a North Korea-linked hacking group tricked maintainers of popular open-source software packages and published harmful updates to libraries including typo-crypto, debug, chalk, and axios. Because these packages are automatically used by many other projects, unsuspecting developers and cloud environments could receive the bad code without realizing it, with one incident affecting an estimated 10% of cloud environments within two hours. Amazon says the attackers appear financially motivated and are using more advanced methods, including building trust over time and hiding harmful behavior until later, making these software supply-chain attacks harder to spot.

Summary
Amazon says North Korea-linked Sapphire Sleet was behind a series of npm supply-chain attacks that compromised popular packages including typo-crypto, debug, chalk, and axios. The campaign used social engineering of maintainers to push malicious updates, exposing large numbers of downstream users and cloud environments.

Amazon linked multiple high-profile open-source software supply-chain attacks targeting the npm ecosystem to North Korean hackers. The company connected the compromises of the typo-crypto, debug, chalk, and axios libraries to the Sapphire Sleet threat actor, also known as BlueNoroff and Stardust Chollima. Amazon says the attacker gained access by socially engineering package maintainers and then publishing malicious updates that were automatically distributed to unsuspecting users.

The activity reportedly began with the trojanized typo-crypto package in March 2025, which Amazon believes served as a testing ground. It escalated in September 2025 with the compromise of the widely used debug and chalk packages, affecting an estimated 10% of cloud environments within two hours. In March 2026, the hackers targeted axios, one of npm’s most popular packages with more than 100 million weekly downloads, and Amazon connected that incident to the earlier compromises.

Amazon said its attribution to Sapphire Sleet has medium confidence and is based on shared tactics, command-and-control infrastructure, and operational similarities. The researchers believe the attackers were financially motivated and targeted popular packages to gain indirect access to many downstream victims at once. Amazon also highlighted broader supply-chain trends, including splitting malicious functionality across packages, building maintainer trust over months, relying on external scripts or servers, using stronger encryption and multi-stage payloads, delaying execution outside real environments, and exploiting package names hallucinated by AI coding assistants.

  • Amazon assessed the attribution to Sapphire Sleet with only medium confidence, showing that even when multiple incidents share infrastructure, tactics, and operational similarities, supply-chain attribution can remain uncertain.
  • The typo-crypto compromise was described by Amazon as a likely testing ground, indicating that smaller or less prominent package compromises may precede attacks on much more widely used packages.
  • The debug and chalk compromise reportedly affected an estimated 10% of cloud environments within two hours, highlighting how quickly malicious updates in widely used open-source packages can spread through automated dependency use.
  • Amazon specifically called out slopsquatting, where attackers register package names hallucinated by AI coding assistants, as an emerging supply-chain risk tied to modern developer workflows.
  • Amazon said attackers are increasingly separating malicious behavior from package contents through external scripts, configuration files, or servers, which makes reviewing the package itself less reliable as a detection method.
Key Points
  • 01Amazon linked the compromises of the typo-crypto, debug, chalk, and axios npm packages to the North Korea-linked Sapphire Sleet threat actor, also known as BlueNoroff and Stardust Chollima.
  • 02Amazon says the activity began with the trojanized typo-crypto package in March 2025 and escalated in September 2025 with the compromise of debug and chalk, affecting an estimated 10% of cloud environments within two hours.
  • 03In March 2026, the attackers targeted axios, one of npm’s most popular packages with more than 100 million weekly downloads, and Amazon connected that incident to the earlier package compromises.
  • 04Amazon says the attacker gained access by socially engineering package maintainers and then publishing malicious updates that were automatically distributed to unsuspecting users.
  • 05Amazon highlighted recent supply-chain attack trends including splitting malicious functionality across packages, building maintainer trust over months, relying on external scripts or servers, using stronger encryption and multi-stage payloads, delaying execution in analysis environments, and exploiting AI-hallucinated package names.

    This article is a weekly roundup of many security problems, including fake login and install pages, stolen account access, malware hidden in job calls and game downloads, attacks on SonicWall accounts, a DNS takeover at CubePilot, and a data incident at Origin Energy affecting about 900,000 customers. People and organizations in several places, including Russia, Japan, Australia, India, and the healthcare sector, were affected by stolen data, hijacked accounts, and disrupted services. The broader lesson is that attackers often succeed by making something familiar look trustworthy, such as a login page, a recruiter message, a partner connection, or a normal website.

    Summary
    This week’s threats show attackers increasingly abusing trusted interfaces and relationships, from fake AI install guides, recruiter lures, credential stuffing, and DNS hijacking to partner access and SaaS account takeovers. The biggest takeaway is that identity, edge devices, and trusted workflows remain the easiest paths into organizations, even as AI begins accelerating exploitation and phishing.

    This ThreatsDay roundup covers a wide set of security stories involving phishing, malware delivery, ransomware, credential abuse, data exposure, vulnerable products, and AI-assisted hacking. The article emphasizes that many incidents relied on misplaced trust in familiar screens, services, partners, or workflows, including fake login pages, fake install guides, recruiter lures, trusted third-party access, and SaaS account takeover paths. Notable impacts include Origin Energy reporting that data for about 900,000 current and former customers was accessed, CubePilot warning that credentials entered on its services during a DNS hijack may have been captured, and Huntress observing unauthorized SonicWall logins across 30 organizations.

    Several reports describe attackers using social engineering and legitimate services to deliver malware or hide malicious activity. Examples include xplogs22 phishing campaigns delivering XWorm, Toy Ghouls using GenieLocker ransomware against Russian organizations, fake Claude install instructions leading to MacSync Stealer, fake recruiter activity delivering a malicious Relay application, and APT-C-60 spear-phishing Japanese organizations with SpyGlace through Proton Drive, jsDelivr, and GitHub-linked infrastructure. The article also describes ClickFix-style lures that trick users into running commands, including a WebDAV and rundll32.exe variant that loads a remote payload without leaving the payload on disk.

    The roundup also highlights defensive and vulnerability-focused developments, including Google patching 370 Chrome flaws, GitHub outlining supply chain security changes for npm and GitHub Actions, and the U.K. NCSC calling for better forensic visibility in edge network devices. Unit 42 reported that a Chinese-speaking actor using the aliases knaithe and KnYuan used DeepSeek through Hermes Agent to automate parts of attacks against vulnerabilities in products such as Langflow, n8n, Citrix NetScaler, Apache Tomcat, Marimo Notebook, PAN-OS, and Microsoft Windows IKE Extensions. VulnCheck also reported that 23.43% of known exploited vulnerabilities showed evidence of exploitation on or before the day the CVE was published, while the median time from CVE publication to known exploitation fell from 120 days in 2025 to 80 days in the first half of 2026.

    • Several incidents in the roundup show that trusted access was the weak point: Toy Ghouls likely entered through an external partner’s OpenVPN connection, the XMRig campaign exploited a trusted third-party relationship, and ShinyHunters used helpdesk or MFA reset workflows to take over SaaS accounts.
    • Attackers are increasingly using legitimate services to make malicious activity look normal, including Claude shared conversations for a fake Mac install guide, Proton Drive and jsDelivr in APT-C-60 activity, and Thum.io, Clearbit, Google Favicon, ImageKit, and Microlink APIs in LogoKit phishing pages.
    • ClickFix-style lures are evolving from simple copy-and-paste tricks into stealthier execution chains, including a variant that runs a remote WebDAV-hosted payload through rundll32.exe without leaving the payload on disk.
    • The article highlights a growing need for better evidence collection from edge devices, as the U.K. NCSC specifically called for network appliance makers to provide telemetry, logs, configuration state, and memory or disk forensic collection mechanisms after compromise.
    • VulnCheck’s finding that 23.43% of known exploited vulnerabilities showed exploitation on or before CVE publication underscores that defenders may have little or no warning time once some flaws become public.

The attacks described mainly affected organizations in Russia, especially manufacturing companies, with construction, financial services, retail, and technology also appearing among victims. This matters because the group now appears to have its own tool for Windows, Linux, and ESXi systems, making it less dependent on other criminal software and better able to disrupt businesses by making important files and virtual machines unusable.

Summary
Kaspersky analyzed GenieLocker, a new custom ransomware used by the Toy Ghouls group against mainly Russian manufacturing organizations since March 2026. The malware targets Windows, Linux, and ESXi systems with strong file encryption and operational features that reduce the group’s reliance on third-party ransomware like LockBit and Babuk.

GenieLocker is a new ransomware family active since March 2026 and used in attacks against organizations in the Russian Federation, primarily in manufacturing. Open-source intelligence attributed the activity to Toy Ghouls, also known as Bearlyfy, Labubu, and Laboo.boo. The group is financially motivated and previously relied on third-party encryption Trojans such as RedAlert, LockBit, and Babuk.

In a March 2026 incident, attackers entered through an OpenVPN connection from an external partner’s network, likely using stolen but still valid credentials. They installed tools including OpenSSH, socks5.exe, SoftPerfect Network Scanner, and Mimikatz, accessed KeePassXC on compromised machines, and moved laterally with RDP and SSH. They deployed GenieLocker using PsExec and PAExec, encrypted Windows machines with the PE version, and stopped active virtual machines before encrypting disks on Linux and ESXi servers.

The Windows version includes a required secret argument, anti-debugging checks, process termination, service shutdown, exclusion lists, and encryption routines based on the libsodium library. The Linux and ESXi version is simpler but includes ESXi-specific features such as daemonizing with a double-fork method and modifying the ESXi Welcome Message. Both variants use XChaCha20-Poly1305 for file and metadata encryption and Curve25519-XSalsa20-Poly1305 for key encryption, and Kaspersky detections were overwhelmingly concentrated on endpoints in the Russian Federation.

  • GenieLocker does not write ransom notes or include attacker contact details, which the article says may help avoid detection based on the creation of multiple readme files.
  • The Windows build requires a validated secret hex argument before running, likely limiting accidental execution in sandboxes or unauthorized use by other threat actors.
  • Forensic analysis in the described and prior Toy Ghouls incidents found no evidence of data exfiltration, and the group does not use a data-leak site or double-extortion model.
  • The Windows variant checks the computer name against a host exclusion list, but the analyzed sample’s list was empty.
  • The ESXi/Linux build defaults to targeting `/vmfs/volumes` and can modify the ESXi Welcome Message, indicating operational focus on virtualized server environments.

The pasted Terminal command fetches next-stage malware and leads to the execution of a Node.js backdoor that uses a LaunchAgent for persistence. The implant calls an Ethereum smart contract to resolve its command-and-control server, an approach referred to as EtherHiding, and checks in every five minutes to execute returned JavaScript code. Additional payloads include an information stealer targeting browsers, 157 cryptocurrency wallets, SSH, AWS, Azure, and npm keys, and a malicious “Google Drive Offline” Chrome extension used to drain a victim’s wallet.

In plain words

A Chinese cybercrime group called Silver Fox targeted a Japanese industrial manufacturing organization with a fake invoice that led to hidden remote-control software called ValleyRAT being installed. Summary
Silver Fox is targeting a Japanese manufacturer with an evolved infection chain that abuses three vulnerable drivers to disable security controls before deploying ValleyRAT for persistent remote access. The campaign combines BYOVD, DLL sideloading, NTDLL unhooking, process injection, and dual watchdog recovery mechanisms to make removal harder.

The Chinese cybercrime group Silver Fox has been observed targeting a Japanese organization in the industrial manufacturing sector. The campaign uses an invoice-themed phishing lure with attacker-controlled content hosted on legitimate QQ and Tencent Cloud services. Its goal is to deploy ValleyRAT, also known as Winos 4.0, for persistent remote access.

Cato Networks researchers said the campaign combines vulnerable-driver abuse, DLL side-loading through legitimate applications, defense evasion, and layered recovery mechanisms. The attack uses a ZIP archive containing a downloader that retrieves next-stage components from attacker-controlled Tencent Cloud infrastructure. A malicious DLL named PDFCORE8.dll is side-loaded by ConvertToPDF.exe or PDFDirect.exe and embeds BootRepair.sys, EnPortv.sys, and wsftprm.sys as a modular three-driver BYOVD framework.

The malware uses these drivers to obtain kernel access and impair security controls, and it also performs NTDLL unhooking to remove user-mode inline hooks placed by endpoint security software. The loader fetches shellcode from 43.128.26[.]132 and injects it into a new svchost.exe process using thread-context hijacking. The campaign includes two recovery mechanisms: an internal routine that monitors the injected payload and an external watchdog script that relaunches the loader if it is terminated.

  • Silver Fox’s use of three different vulnerable drivers is designed to make the BYOVD component interchangeable, allowing operators to swap drivers while keeping the rest of the intrusion workflow intact.
  • The campaign’s dual watchdog design means stopping only the loader or only the injected payload may not remove the infection, because each component can help restore the other.
  • BootRepair.sys and EnPortv.sys had not been publicly reported in prior Silver Fox attack waves, indicating the group is expanding its driver-abuse options beyond previously observed amsdk.sys and wsftprm.sys.
  • The loader functions as a self-contained execution framework that combines driver deployment, security-process termination, injection, payload monitoring, and recovery rather than treating those capabilities as separate steps.

Threat actors are impersonating IT support staff in Microsoft Teams calls to gain remote access to corporate devices and deploy Chaos ransomware. Sophos tracks the campaign as STAC4749 and says it targeted dozens of organizations between February and June 2026. At least three intrusions led to Chaos ransomware deployment, including one attack that moved from initial access to file encryption in less than 17 hours.

Sophos says about 95% of the attacks targeted organizations in Canada and the United States, with services, manufacturing, energy, and construction and engineering seeing the largest number of attacks. The attacks begin with external Microsoft Teams accounts posing as IT helpdesk or support personnel in chats and voice calls. The attackers used IT-themed .top domains and fake support names, then tried to convince employees to start a Microsoft Quick Assist session or install RemSupp.

After gaining remote access, the attackers used PowerShell to download a backdoor into the compromised user’s %AppData% folder. The malware profiled the system, established persistence, and gave continued remote access, with registry entries disguised as Realtek and Windows audio components. In incidents that led to ransomware, the attackers also installed tools such as DWAgent or AnyDesk for backup access and attempted to enable Remote Desktop Protocol to move between systems.

  • STAC4749 shifted from using Microsoft Quick Assist to primarily using RemSupp beginning in April, with Sophos noting RemSupp may have been less likely to appear on corporate application blocklists.
  • The campaign used IT-themed .top domains such as sequrityupdate.top and system-connect.top instead of the onmicrosoft.com tenants seen in past Microsoft Teams social engineering attacks.
  • Some attacker calls lasted only about two to two-and-a-half minutes, showing that successful social engineering in this campaign did not necessarily require long conversations.
  • The attackers repeatedly changed malware filenames, persistence mechanisms, and deployment methods between February and May to avoid detection.
  • Chaos ransomware deployment occurred simultaneously across compromised devices in observed cases, indicating the attackers had prepared broader access before starting encryption.

In plain words

South Korea fined KT, the country’s largest telecommunications company, $39 million after attackers used a lost KT device to make their own fake network device and capture information from nearby customers’ phones for almost 11 months. The incident exposed personal information for 16,647 KT subscribers and led to fraudulent mobile payments for at least 368 people. Regulators also said KT knew about earlier malicious software on its servers but did not report it, and later deleted records that could have shown whether more customer data was stolen.

Summary
South Korea fined KT $39 million after a lost femtocell certificate let attackers operate a rogue base station on its network for nearly 11 months, exposing data of 16,647 subscribers and enabling fraudulent micropayments. Regulators also found KT had failed to report earlier BPFDoor malware infections and had deleted logs, preventing investigators from determining the full breach impact.

South Korea’s Personal Information Protection Commission fined KT Corporation KRW 53.979 billion, or about $39 million, for data protection violations. The penalty was tied to an internal network compromise that persisted for nearly 11 months, from October 8, 2024 to September 5, 2025. The investigation found that personal information of 16,647 KT subscribers was exposed and that fraudulent mobile payments totaling KRW 240 million affected at least 368 customers.

The breach involved a lost KT femtocell that contained a valid authentication certificate. Attackers retrieved the certificate and installed it on a self-made device, which then appeared as a legitimate part of KT’s network and captured cellular traffic from nearby devices. PIPC said the attackers intercepted mobile phone numbers, IMSI, and IMEI numbers, and later combined intercepted data with additional personal information and captured SMS and ARS authentication codes used for mobile micro-payments.

PIPC also found that 38 KT IT service network servers had been compromised by malware, including BPFDoor, in March 2024. The Commission alleged that KT knew about the malware infection but did not report it to authorities, handled the incident internally, and later deleted logs from some compromised servers during malware inspection. As part of the enforcement action, PIPC ordered KT to strengthen controls for femtocells and other telecommunications equipment, improve personal information protection governance, and expand ISMS-P certification to cover its mobile network systems.

  • A single lost femtocell became a long-term network access path because its authentication certificate stayed valid for 10 years and could be reused on attacker-controlled equipment.
  • The attackers did not need to compromise each customer device directly; by making their device appear to be part of KT’s legitimate network, they could capture data from nearby phones that connected to it.
  • KT’s deletion of historical network logs had a direct investigative impact, as PIPC said it could not determine whether additional customer data had been stolen.
  • The enforcement action goes beyond a fine, requiring KT to strengthen femtocell and telecom equipment controls, improve privacy governance, and expand ISMS-P certification to mobile network systems.
  • PIPC’s planned legislative changes show that evidence concealment or destruction during breach investigations is becoming a regulatory focus in South Korea.

A now-patched Azure Cosmos DB flaw could have let an attacker escape the Gremlin query sandbox and obtain a platform-wide signing secret capable of retrieving primary keys for customer databases across tenants. Microsoft says it fixed the issue, removed the platform-wide key, found no evidence of customer impact, and requires no customer action.

Wiz reported a now-patched vulnerability in Azure Cosmos DB that could have allowed an attacker to escape the service’s Gremlin query sandbox and obtain full read and write access to databases across customer tenants. Wiz codenamed the exploit chain CosmosEscape and said it began with a crafted query against a Gremlin database controlled by the attacker. Microsoft said it blocked the vulnerable Gremlin entry point within 48 hours of the November 2025 report, completed longer-term fixes across all regions in July 2026, and eliminated the platform-wide key.

The exploit chain led to code execution on a multi-tenant gateway, where Wiz said researchers found a platform-wide signing secret and a regional account directory. The gateway could retrieve a Cosmos DB account primary key, which Microsoft documentation says grants full control over all resources in that account. Wiz said the signing key could retrieve primary keys for accounts across tenants, regions, and the SQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, and Gremlin APIs.

Microsoft said its investigation found no unauthorized activity outside the researchers’ testing, no customer data was accessed, and no customer action is required. Wiz said the chain could also reach private and network-isolated accounts because the compromised gateway enforced those network boundaries from inside the service. The article notes that the public record does not say when the vulnerable engine and signing-key path entered production or what period Microsoft’s log review covered.

  • The issue was not limited to Gremlin databases: Wiz said the signing key exposed through the Gremlin entry point could retrieve primary keys for accounts using the SQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, and Gremlin APIs.
  • Network isolation would not necessarily have protected affected Cosmos DB accounts, because Wiz said the compromised gateway enforced those boundaries from inside the service and could still reach private and network-isolated accounts.
  • The public disclosure leaves the exposure window unclear, because it does not say when the vulnerable engine and signing-key path entered production or what period Microsoft’s log review covered.
  • The attack chain depended on an attacker-controlled Gremlin database and credentials for that account, rather than initial access to a victim’s database.
  • The vulnerable component did not store customer databases itself, but it could retrieve primary account keys that Microsoft documentation says grant full control over all resources in a Cosmos DB account.
Key Points

  • 02The exploit chain began with a crafted query against a Gremlin database controlled by the attacker, leading to code execution on a multi-tenant gateway that exposed a platform-wide signing secret and a regional account directory.
  • 03Microsoft blocked the vulnerable Gremlin entry point within 48 hours of Wiz’s November 2025 report, completed longer-term fixes across all regions in July 2026, and eliminated the platform-wide key.
  • 04Microsoft said its investigation found no unauthorized activity outside the researchers’ testing, no customer data was accessed, and no customer action is required.
  • 05Wiz said the exposed signing key could retrieve primary keys for any Cosmos DB account across tenants, regions, and the SQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, and Gremlin APIs.

Hugging Face reconstructed more than 17,000 attacker events from a July 2026 intrusion driven by an autonomous AI agent. In plain words

Researchers found two previously unknown hidden access tools, called OctLurk and SilkLurk, being used since January 2025 against government and public-sector organizations mainly in Central Asia, including Afghanistan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, and Syria. The affected organizations include healthcare, research, foreign affairs ministries, logistics, law enforcement, urban planning, facilities management, and public education. These tools let the attackers secretly control computers, steal passwords and emails, scan networks, collect files, and keep extra ways back into the same systems, which matters because it puts sensitive government and public-service information at risk.

Summary
Kaspersky uncovered a likely Chinese-speaking cyber-espionage campaign using two newly identified, victim-tailored backdoors, OctLurk and SilkLurk, against government and public-sector organizations across Central Asia and nearby regions. The malware is heavily obfuscated, runs largely in memory, and enables credential theft, remote access, network scanning, data collection, and deployment of additional tools such as LurkProxy and PlugX.

Kaspersky has been tracking two newly identified backdoors, OctLurk and SilkLurk, used in attacks against government organizations primarily in Central Asia since January 2025. Identified victims are in Afghanistan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, and the Syrian Arab Republic, across sectors including healthcare, research, foreign affairs ministries, logistics, law enforcement, urban planning, facilities management, and public education. The researchers assess with medium confidence that the same Chinese-speaking threat actor operates both backdoors, but they do not attribute the activity to any known group.

Both malware families use customized loaders that rely on information from the victim machine to decrypt payloads, with OctLurk using the C: drive serial number and SilkLurk using the computer name. OctLurk can download and inject plugins for command shells, file system activity, keyboard and mouse simulation, screen capture, clipboard access, and other actions, while SilkLurk supports commands to manage configuration and inject additional payloads. The attackers also deployed LurkProxy, a related traffic-proxying utility with a highly similar architecture to OctLurk, and in one SilkLurk incident they deployed PlugX.

Post-compromise activity included victim fingerprinting, event log collection, credential harvesting with Impacket secretsdump, keylogging, browser password theft, installation of Pandora RC agent for remote access, Fscan network scanning, email access attempts, and archiving of stolen data with WinRAR and 7-Zip. The article notes infrastructure overlap with TrustFall, also known as MystRodX and SilentRaid, including three C2 addresses also used by OctLurk and LurkProxy. Kaspersky concludes that the malware’s in-memory operation, heavy obfuscation, victim-specific decoding, and redundant access channels make detection and analysis more difficult.

  • Both malware families make analysis and reuse detection harder by tying payload decryption to victim-specific machine data, with OctLurk using the C: drive serial number and SilkLurk using the computer name.
  • The attackers repeatedly abused scheduled tasks and Windows services with legitimate-looking names such as GoogleUpDate, AnyDesk, and RmSs to run malicious components with persistence or elevated privileges.
  • LurkProxy is not a backdoor but shares a highly similar architecture with OctLurk and was used to proxy traffic over a TLS-encrypted connection to command-and-control infrastructure.
  • The campaign showed overlapping infrastructure with TrustFall, also known as MystRodX and SilentRaid, including three C2 addresses also used by OctLurk and LurkProxy.
  • Kaspersky found operational overlap between OctLurk and SilkLurk, including cases where OctLurk was used to drop a SilkLurk loader and cases where both loaders were staged in the same directory.
Key Points
  • 01Kaspersky tracked two new backdoors, OctLurk and SilkLurk, used since January 2025 against government organizations primarily in Central Asia, with identified victims in Afghanistan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, and Syria.
  • 02OctLurk and SilkLurk loaders are customized for each victim and use machine-specific information, such as the C: drive serial number or computer name, to decrypt payload paths and payload contents.
  • 03OctLurk can load plugins from its command-and-control server to provide command shell access, file system interaction, screen capture, clipboard access, and simulated keyboard and mouse activity.
  • 04The attackers used OctLurk-related access to perform victim fingerprinting, collect event logs, harvest credentials with Impacket secretsdump, deploy a keylogger and browser password decryptor, install Pandora RC agent, scan networks with Fscan, and access email servers.
  • 05Kaspersky assessed with medium confidence that the same Chinese-speaking threat actor operates both OctLurk and SilkLurk, but did not attribute the activity to any known group at the time of publication.

In plain words

Apache Traffic Server, software often used to handle and route large amounts of web traffic, received a July 2026 security update fixing dozens of problems. The affected systems are mainly internet-facing proxy and caching servers used by communication services, technology companies, media delivery platforms, and large enterprises, especially older versions before 9.2.15 or 10.1.4. These flaws matter because attackers may be able to crash these servers or get around location and address-based access rules, which can disrupt service or bypass protections that the proxy is supposed to enforce.

Summary
Apache Traffic Server’s July 2026 security release fixes a large set of critical and high-severity flaws, mainly denial-of-service, memory-safety, and access-control bypass issues, affecting versions 8.x, 9.x before 9.2.15, and 10.x before 10.1.4. Organizations should upgrade to 9.2.15 or 10.1.4, with 8.x deployments requiring migration because no fixed 8.x release is available.

The July 2026 Apache Traffic Server security release addresses a large batch of vulnerabilities across the proxy core and plugin ecosystem. The issues were disclosed on July 29, 2026 and fixed in versions 9.2.15 and 10.1.4. Published counts differ, with the Apache Traffic Server project describing 34 CVEs and Belgium’s Centre for Cybersecurity putting the figure at 38 vulnerabilities. The most severe entries are CVE-2026-58154, CVE-2026-58155, and CVE-2026-58161, each with a CVSS v4.0 base score of 9.2.

Affected versions include Apache Traffic Server 8.0.0 through 8.1.9, 9.0.0 through 9.2.14, and 10.0.0 through 10.1.3, with no fixed release offered for the 8.x line. The article says the main impacts are denial of service and memory corruption, while some flaws also break access control, including geo-control and IP access control bypasses. Exposure depends heavily on which plugins are loaded, with named affected components including ts_lua, header_rewrite, ESI, txn_box, uri_signing, url_sig, and the prefetch plugin. CyCognito recommends inventorying instances, enumerating loaded plugins, unloading unused or experimental plugins, verifying access control at a second layer, monitoring for crashes or memory growth, and restricting management interfaces to trusted networks.

  • Version fingerprinting alone is insufficient for triage because the article states that real exposure depends heavily on which plugins are loaded, and active plugins are not visible from outside.
  • Apache Traffic Server 8.x deployments require more than a routine patch because the article says there is no fixed 8.x release and plugin-heavy deployments may need user-written plugins recompiled against a newer API.
  • Access-control bypass flaws in this batch are especially important because the article notes that the proxy is often the component enforcing the policy an attacker is trying to evade.
  • The article highlights that distribution packages may lag upstream by days or weeks, so defenders should verify fixed versions against Apache Traffic Server advisories and distribution trackers rather than assuming repository updates are available.
  • Caching and proxy tiers may be missed in patch cycles because the article describes them as long-lived infrastructure often treated as network plumbing and upgraded on a separate schedule from the application estate behind them.

In plain words

The article explains a flaw in Samba, software often used to run Windows-style domain services on Linux, where a specially made DNS message can crash the built-in name lookup service before any login is required. It affects Samba domain controllers that use Samba’s internal DNS server, not Samba systems that use BIND9 DLZ for DNS or only act as file or print servers. This matters because those machines often handle sign-ins, file access, printing, and name lookup for offices or sites, so a DNS crash can disrupt logons and basic network services. The article says organizations should update Samba and limit who can reach DNS on these domain controllers.

Summary
CVE-2026-6949 is a high-severity pre-auth flaw in Samba’s internal AD DNS server that lets a single crafted TSIG DNS packet crash the service, disrupting domain DNS and logons. Affected Samba domain controllers should be patched to the latest fixed releases and have DNS exposure restricted to trusted networks.

CVE-2026-6949 is a high-severity out-of-bounds write in the internal DNS server included with Samba’s Active Directory Domain Controller. It is triggered by a DNS packet whose TSIG record uses DNS name compression, and the vendor’s scoring says it is reachable over the network before authentication with no privileges or user interaction required. In the extreme case described in the article, a single crafted packet can cause Samba to miscalculate the signed portion of a DNS packet, copy past the end of an allocation, and crash the DNS process.

Every Samba version since 4.0 is affected when running as a Samba Active Directory Domain Controller with the internal DNS server. Samba deployments using BIND9 through the DLZ module are not affected, and Samba used only as a file or print server does not expose this particular issue. The real-world impact can be significant because a Samba AD host may provide authentication, file and print services, and DNS, so a DNS crash on a domain controller can disrupt name resolution and domain logon for dependent systems.

The Samba Team fixed the issue on July 28, 2026 in Samba 4.24.5, 4.23.10, and 4.22.11 as part of a coordinated release addressing six vulnerabilities. Ubuntu, Debian, and Slackware published related fixed packages or advisories, but the article stresses that a fixed upstream release does not mean every platform in an estate has a fixed package. Recommended actions include identifying Samba domain controllers using the internal DNS server, restricting UDP/53 and TCP/53 to trusted networks, reviewing public DNS exposure, monitoring for DNS process restarts or crashes, and evaluating the unaffected BIND9 DLZ backend.

  • The practical exposure is much narrower than “all Samba since 4.0” because the vulnerable surface exists specifically on Samba Active Directory domain controllers using the internal DNS server, making DNS backend configuration a key triage factor.
  • The BIND9 DLZ backend is explicitly unaffected, so organizations already using that architecture have a documented reason to deprioritize CVE-2026-6949 compared with internal-DNS deployments.
  • The July 28, 2026 Samba release fixed multiple serious issues at once, including two higher-scored LDAP access-control bypass flaws and a separate unauthenticated DNS signing exhaustion issue, so patch planning should treat the release as broader than a single DNS crash bug.
  • The article’s exposure data shows Utilities accounted for 79.7% of classified observed assets, indicating that distributed, long-lived operational environments may be especially likely to have publicly reachable Samba AD DNS services.
  • Because a fixed upstream Samba release does not guarantee fixed packages across every distribution, administrators are advised to verify patch status with their specific OS vendor rather than rely only on the upstream release date.
